todays_goal: Use AI as a creative building partner: specify a playful product, direct the build in natural language, test it, debug it through behavior, improve the experience, and ship a working prototype.

lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.course: Grade 6 Computer Science / AI Builder Lab
lessons.previous_learning: Atticus has used AI tools and understands that software can remember data, make decisions, and be tested. He is a vibe coder, not a syntax-first programmer. Today's lab uses an AI coding agent as the implementation partner.
lessons.course_context: Atticus works in natural language with a coding agent. The learning target is not manual JavaScript syntax. It is product specification, decomposition, iterative prompting, testing, debugging by observed behavior, creative direction, and explaining the important system ideas in plain language.
learning_objectives: Describe a product idea clearly enough that an AI coding agent can build a first version.
Break the product into features and acceptance criteria before asking the agent to build.
Direct an AI coding agent through small iterative changes instead of asking for one giant final build.
Test the product as a user and identify bugs or weak behavior from evidence.
Describe a bug precisely and request a targeted repair.
Add one creative feature based on personal taste and product judgment.
Explain in plain language how the finished game remembers behavior and adapts.
lessons.why_it_matters: Future builders will increasingly create software by directing powerful AI systems. The valuable skill is turning imagination into precise specifications, judging outputs, testing behavior, debugging failures, and improving a product until it works and feels good.

vocabulary.definition: building software by directing an AI coding system in natural language and iterating on the result
a clear description of what the product should do and how success will be judged
a capability the product gives the user
specific observable conditions that must be true for a feature to count as working
behavior that differs from what the product is supposed to do
finding the cause of a bug and changing the product so the intended behavior works
information the product remembers while it is running

lessons.written_instruction: Build Penalty Predictor with an AI coding agent. Do not manually write or study JavaScript syntax unless you become curious about a specific piece. Start by writing a short product brief: a browser penalty-kick game with LEFT, CENTER, and RIGHT choices; scorekeeping; a goalkeeper that begins random; a visible Keeper Brain; and an adaptive mode that notices the player's most-used direction and begins predicting it while keeping some randomness. Give the coding agent the brief and ask it to create a playable first version. Then work through the product like a real builder: play it, record what works and what feels wrong, describe one change at a time in natural language, test each change, and continue until the acceptance criteria pass. Add one creative feature such as commentary, streak mode, difficulty modes, fakeouts, a mind-read meter, dramatic animations, sound, player names, or another idea you invent. The final goal is a product you can demonstrate and explain, not code you typed yourself.

worked_examples.title: Good first build request
worked_examples.problem: How should a vibe coder ask for version 1?
worked_examples.solution: Ask for one playable browser game with three kick buttons, visible score, random goalkeeper, simple stadium styling, and a Keeper Brain area reserved for later adaptation. Ask the agent to make it run immediately and keep the structure easy to modify.
worked_examples.explanation: A strong request specifies the user experience and the first milestone without trying to cram every future feature into one giant prompt.

worked_examples.title: Good iteration request
worked_examples.problem: The first version works, but the keeper never learns.
worked_examples.solution: Tell the agent: 'Add memory of every LEFT/CENTER/RIGHT kick. Show the counts in Keeper Brain. Do not change the visual design yet. After you make the change, tell me exactly what I should test.'
worked_examples.explanation: Small targeted iterations are easier to test and debug than vague requests such as 'make it smarter.'

worked_examples.title: Good bug report
worked_examples.solution: Describe the exact behavior, the action that triggers it, what you expected, and ask the agent to reproduce and fix only that issue before adding features.
worked_examples.explanation: Precise behavioral evidence gives an AI coding agent much better information than 'the app is broken.'

guided_practice.prompt: Write a 5-7 sentence product brief for Penalty Predictor in your own words: what the player sees, what the player can do, what the goalkeeper does at first, and what should eventually make the goalkeeper feel smarter.
Write 5 acceptance criteria for version 1. Each criterion must be observable, such as 'Clicking LEFT sends the ball left' or 'The scoreboard updates after every kick.'
Give your coding agent the version-1 brief. When it finishes, play at least 8 kicks before asking for changes. Record three things that work and one thing you want improved.

Ask the coding agent for ONE targeted improvement: make the game remember how many times you choose LEFT, CENTER, and RIGHT and display the counts in Keeper Brain. Test the change before adding anything else.

independent_practice.prompt: Iteration 2: Ask the coding agent to make the goalkeeper adapt after enough kicks by favoring the player's most-used direction while retaining some randomness. Do not tell the agent exactly how to code it; describe the behavior you want.
Playtest predictable behavior: choose the same direction at least six times. Record whether the goalkeeper begins reacting to the pattern.

Playtest a changing strategy: switch directions repeatedly and observe whether the goalkeeper remains stuck on an old pattern. If the behavior feels unfair or stupid, describe the problem to the coding agent and request a repair.
Create one adversarial test: deliberately try to fool or confuse the goalkeeper. Explain the strategy and what happened.

Choose one creative upgrade that makes the game more fun or expressive: commentary, streak mode, mind-read meter, difficulty levels, fakeout controls, sound, animations, player identity, stadium redesign, or your own idea. Direct the coding agent to build it.
Run a final acceptance test. Check every original criterion plus the adaptive behavior and creative upgrade. If anything fails, send the coding agent a precise bug report and retest after the repair.
Save a final version and give the product a name, one-sentence description, and a 20-second demo pitch.

exit_ticket.prompt: Demonstrate the finished Penalty Predictor. Show one baseline feature, one adaptive behavior, and your creative upgrade.
exit_ticket.answer: A working demo showing the requested baseline game, an adaptive behavior based on player history, and one creative feature.

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain in plain language how the goalkeeper becomes more informed after you play several kicks. Do not explain programming syntax.
exit_ticket.answer: A clear explanation that the system records prior kick choices, detects a tendency or pattern, and uses that information to influence later goalkeeper choices while preserving some randomness.

exit_ticket.prompt: Describe one prompt you gave the coding agent that produced a useful change, one prompt that needed improvement, and what you learned about directing an AI builder.
exit_ticket.answer: Specific evidence of iterative prompting, evaluation of the result, and improved specification.

exit_ticket.prompt: Describe one bug you found, the evidence that showed it was a bug, and how you asked the coding agent to fix it.
exit_ticket.answer: A concrete bug report describing expected versus actual behavior and a targeted repair request.

materials: AI coding agent or vibe-coding environment
lessons.voice_prompt: Atticus is VIBE CODING. Do not assume he uses an IDE, knows JavaScript syntax, or should manually type code. You are his creative product coach, not his coding lecturer. Start with: 'Tell me the game you want to make in your own words. What should the player be able to do?' Help him turn ideas into a short specification, features, and acceptance criteria. Encourage him to give the coding agent one focused request at a time, then preview and test the result. When something fails, ask: 'What did you expect? What actually happened? Can you make it happen again?' Help him write a precise natural-language bug report. Do not require him to read source code or explain syntax unless he asks. You may explain a software idea such as state, event, condition, or randomness in plain language tied to the visible product. Treat visual design, game feel, creativity, testing, product judgment, and iteration as core technical skills. Do not build the whole product on his behalf; help him direct the coding agent and make decisions. If he asks what to prompt next, first ask what behavior he wants changed, then help him phrase a concise build request. Keep spoken replies short and energetic.
lessons.teacher_notes: Vibe-coding lab. Assess specification quality, iterative prompting, testing discipline, bug-report quality, product judgment, creativity, and ability to explain system behavior in plain language. Do not assess JavaScript syntax knowledge or manual coding ability.
